prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms made fractional uncertainties of 10^-18 reproducibly attainable

statement.case_for: I keep B024 as a stand-alone prize and my configuration has not changed since round 1. After the exchange I think the case is stronger on the one point where it was attacked hardest, namely discovery versus technology. A lattice clock is not simply a better version of an old clock. The magic-wavelength condition lets one hold of order a million neutral atoms in a lattice with the trapping light shift cancelled, and that is what turned a counting-statistics problem into a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and below. It is also what made new physics accessible in the laboratory: centimetre-scale gravitational redshift measured across a single atomic sample, many-body and spin-exchange effects that had to be understood to reach the accuracy, and long-baseline comparisons between sites that set limits on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter. The result has been reproduced and surpassed independently at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, with agreement at the 10^-18 level, which is the test of reproducibility I give most weight. Attribution is two names for two distinct contributions, the proposal with first demonstration and the systematics and coherence programme that proved the accuracy. I accept that this is a prize for a measurement capability, and I think the statutes' reference to discovery or invention allows that, in the same tradition as earlier prizes for instruments that changed what could be observed.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one Danielsson, Olsson, Lindroth and Eriksson all press: so far the clocks have delivered limits and an instrument, not a new fact about nature, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. A committee that wants a discovery about nature could fairly prefer B020 or B025. The 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes sit nearby, so the citation has to rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime and not on optical frequency metrology in general. Priority is not fully clean: the idea of using neutral atoms in a lattice at a magic wavelength has parallel and earlier threads (Lemonde and collaborators, and the earlier ion-clock and lattice work), and I am relying on memory for the detailed chronology, so I cannot call the Katori-Ye split verified. Finally, I recognise that Ludlow, Hinkley, Campbell and colleagues, and other national laboratories, did essential work that three names cannot capture, although here two names are enough to represent the core.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether the Katori-Ye split is robust against the Lemonde and Gill priority argument, and asked that the citation rest on the lattice and 10^-18 rather than on frequency metrology generally.
responses.response: My answer is that the split is robust for the specific claim I would put in the citation, but not against a broad claim of having invented neutral-atom optical clocks. Katori's contribution is the magic-wavelength lattice concept, developed around 2001 to 2003, together with the early strontium demonstrations in Tokyo. Ye's contribution is the experimental programme at JILA that took the clock to 10^-18, with the density, blackbody-shift and coherence work that made the accuracy credible. Proposals for lattice clocks with neutral atoms existed in other groups, and Lemonde, Gill and others did important work on the neutral-atom and ion routes, so a citation that says 'optical clocks' would be attackable. A citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice and 10^-18 is not, and that is the wording I have used. I therefore agree with his condition and I have tightened my own citation to meet it. I also welcome his move toward B024, but I do not follow him to a pairing with B052, because the one-name IceCube credit he concedes is weak would make the two-part prize weaker than B024 alone.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B025 first as a decisive observation that nature delivered, and says he would be persuaded on B024 only if a clock comparison found varying constants or a dark-matter signal.
responses.response: I understand the standard, and I agree that an afterglow redshift is a cleaner example of nature answering a question. I do not agree that a null result is no result. Clock comparisons at 10^-18 have already excluded regions of parameter space for varying constants and for ultralight dark-matter couplings that no earlier technique could reach, and these are measured bounds, not speculation. Whether to wait for a positive signal is a real disagreement between us, and I would not wait, since a positive signal may never arrive. On B025 I accept that it is scientifically strong and fully mature. My doubt is the attribution you also name: the X-ray localisation by Costa and Frontera and the optical and redshift step are separable contributions, and Kulkarni's group did not make the first optical identification or the first redshift. A trio that omits van Paradijs and the Groot-led and Caltech colleagues is exposed to challenge. I would rank it above B021 and below B020 in my alternatives only if the committee could agree on who is credited, and I have not seen that settled.

responses.point: Olsson argues the prize should go to the original idea and first realisation, not to the best number, and favours B005 for its concrete verified effect and broader consequence.
responses.response: Her criterion actually helps B024 more than she suggests. The achievement I am crediting is the idea and first realisation of a clock in which the lattice does not perturb the transition, which is Katori, plus the demonstration that this concept survives a full systematics analysis at 10^-18, which is Ye. The best number is the evidence of the concept, not the concept itself. I also accept her point that B005 is a finished, replicated discovery with real device consequences. My difficulty is that the 2007 prize on giant magnetoresistance already covers the spintronics sequence, and her own concern about Parkin versus Yuasa and Djayaprawira on the MgO step shows that the attribution is less clean than for the clocks. If the committee prefers a verified discovery with consequences outside physics, B005 is defensible, but I would put it behind B024 on attribution.

responses.point: Johansson asked me whether the lattice-clock result opened new physics or perfected an existing method, and said she would prefer the experimental trio Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger for B020.
responses.response: Both, and the combination is the point. The method was perfected, but the perfection crossed a threshold where new measurements became possible: height differences of centimetres through gravitational redshift, interrogation of many-body interactions inside the clock itself, and continental fibre comparisons that probe fundamental constants. I do not think a clean line separates opening a regime from perfecting a method, which I would say also of the quantum-gas microscope. I agree with her on the experimental trio for B020, and I say again that if the committee prefers a prize about a tunable many-body system, Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger is the allocation I would defend over adding Zoller. Where I remain with B024 is the maturity of the confirmation. The Hubbard programme still lacks its headline answer on the doped model, whereas the clock result has been checked by independent laboratories at the quoted precision.

responses.point: Lindroth holds that the Mott observation is a joint result of the Jaksch-Zoller proposal and the experiment, so one theory name should stay in B020 (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller).
responses.response: The argument is serious, and I accept that without the proposal the experiment would not have been designed in that form. My worry is practical: Zoller and Cirac also appear in the trapped-ion candidate B006, and Jaksch and Hansch fall outside the list, so a theory slot in B020 cannot be filled without a visible arbitrary choice. She herself says that if the committee wants a sharply bounded result, B024 is the better fit, and I would take that as an agreement on what is required of a prize this year. I leave B020 as my first alternative, so my position does not depend on resolving this allocation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a measurement-capability prize in a year when B020, B021 and B025 can be framed as discoveries about nature, and whether others will wait for the redefinition of the second.
The priority chronology of the neutral-atom lattice clock proposal, which I have not been able to verify beyond memory, and thus the exact balance between Katori and Ye.
Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make the committee regard B024 as an extension of already honoured work, despite the distinct magic-wavelength concept.
If B024 does not lead, which alternative is least bad: B020 has an unresolved name allocation and a pending doped-Hubbard payoff, and B002 comes soon after the 2025 circuit prize.
statement.conflict_note: No change in my disclosure and no recusal-level conflict. I spent a year of my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is a later JILA colleague of Hall's, a distant scientific lineage with no collaboration, shared funding or institutional tie to Katori or Ye that I know of. My field, atomic physics and quantum optics at Lund, is close to B024, B020, B006, B002 and B043, so I am not a neutral outsider on these candidates, and colleagues should weigh my views on them with that in mind.
